site-0022.description: Limones preserves a Classic-period stepped pyramid within the modern town of the same name in southern Quintana Roo. Much of the associated settlement remains buried, so the visible monument represents only part of the archaeological record. Its rounded architectural corners have been compared with nearby Chacchoben. That resemblance suggests regional connections but does not, by itself, prove political dependence. The site offers a compact example of Maya monumental architecture surviving within a continuously changing inhabited landscape.

site-0056.description: Tzendales appears in early twentieth-century accounts of the Lacandon forest. Alfred Tozzer described substantial buildings and a carved stela near the Tzendales River, but later literature notes uncertainty about the precise location and condition of the remains. This atlas preserves the historical survey point rather than presenting it as a recently verified position. The entry is useful as a documentary record, with its geographic uncertainty made explicit.

site-0070.description: Pusilhá was a Late Classic kingdom in southern Belize, positioned between river routes linking the central lowlands and the southeastern Maya region. Its inscribed monuments preserve rulers, ceremonies and dynastic history on a scale unusual for a smaller centre. Research has challenged the assumption that such settlements must have been absorbed by powerful neighbours, finding evidence for political independence. Investigations began with a British Museum expedition in 1927, which removed several stelae; later work has examined the city’s architecture, households and regional exchange.

site-0099.description: Yaxuná was linked to Cobá by an exceptionally long raised road crossing the northern Yucatán. Its earlier architecture includes triadic groups, while later rebuilding and fortifications reflect changing political relationships. The settlement stood south of Chichén Itzá and became involved in the competition between that centre and Cobá. Its long occupation makes it useful for tracing how road connections, royal monuments and defensive construction changed over time within the same city.

site-0217.description: Chutixtiox is a fortified Postclassic settlement above the Río Negro near Sacapulas. Cliffs protect three sides, while a narrow approach, ditch and masonry defences controlled access to its plaza and acropolis. Ceramics and architectural changes indicate growing connections with the K’iche’ capital at Q’umarkaj during its later occupation. The site’s layout combines temples, long buildings and a ballcourt in a constrained hilltop setting, making it useful for studying both local traditions and expanding highland political influence.

site-0259.description: El Perú, known anciently as Waka', occupied a strategic position near the San Pedro River west of Tikal. Its court shifted from connections with Tikal toward an alliance with Calakmul. A royal marriage involving Lady T'abi, illustrates the importance of dynastic ties in this political network. Archaeological work on monuments and royal burials has helped recover the history behind the site's modern survey name.

site-0270.description: El Porvenir lies near the Usumacinta and has been interpreted as a point where travellers carried watercraft overland to avoid difficult river passages. This proposed transport role connects the site to the practical geography of river exchange. An inscribed fragment names Ha' K'in Xook, a ruler of nearby Piedras Negras, indicating a relationship with that court. The route interpretation is attributed to research rather than treated as an independently established function of every structure.

site-0275.description: Altar de Sacrificios occupies a strategically important setting near the meeting of the Pasión and Salinas rivers, where they form the Usumacinta. Ceremonial buildings stand on higher ground, with residential areas extending across the surrounding island-like terrain. Excavation documents a long occupation beginning in the Preclassic. The modern name arose from an early interpretation of a monument and should not be read as the ancient name of the city.

site-0278.description: La Amelia was a small Late Classic centre in Guatemala’s lower Pasión region, linked politically to the kingdom ruled from Dos Pilas and later Aguateca. Its carved stairway and panels preserve unusually specific evidence for local rulership during that kingdom’s final decades. Inscriptions name Lachan K’awiil Ajaw Bot and record ceremonies in the early ninth century. Monument building continued into AD 807, making La Amelia an important witness to political activity shortly before the regional settlement system broke apart.

site-0283.description: Tres Islas is a small settlement on the Pasión River whose three stelae and altar carry disproportionate historical importance. Dated Early Classic monuments connect it with emblems later associated with Cancuén and Machaquilá. Their arrangement also recalls the spatial pattern of an E-Group ceremonial complex. The site helps trace the earlier history of regional rulership and exchange before the larger Late Classic centres took their better-known forms.

site-0284.description: Cancuén controlled an important position on the Pasión River and participated in exchange involving jade, obsidian and pyrite. A vast palace associated with Tajal Chan Ahk expresses the wealth of its Late Classic court. Its architecture places unusual emphasis on palatial space rather than great temple pyramids. Evidence of violent deaths near the end of its occupation documents an abrupt political crisis around 800 CE, followed by abandonment.

site-0444.description: Cerro Quiac occupies a steep highland ridge overlooking the Plains of Urbina near Cantel, Guatemala. Two modest architectural groups and eroded stone sculptures distinguish this small ceremonial place from the great lowland cities. Archaeological ceramics and colonial accounts connect its history to the Postclassic highlands and relations between Mam and K’iche’ communities. Local traditions attach additional meanings to the hill, which remains a place of Maya ritual; those traditions should be distinguished from excavated evidence.

site-0482.description: Tak'alik Ab'aj lies on Guatemala's Pacific side along a long-distance exchange corridor linking regions from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec toward El Salvador. Its monuments and material culture document interaction between Olmec traditions and the emergence of early Maya culture. Terraces, sacred spaces and water-management works reveal careful planning, while stone sculpture and worked precious materials record skilled production. The site's importance extends beyond a simple boundary between cultures: it shows how ideas and practices circulated through exchange. Indigenous communities continue to regard the place as sacred and to conduct rituals there.

site-0501.description: Chocolá was an important Preclassic settlement beneath Guatemala’s volcanic highlands, with much of its development between about 1000 BC and AD 200. Excavations revealed monumental platforms, residential areas and a sophisticated network of stone-lined water channels. These works connected settlement planning with the management of abundant local water. Cacao residues in ancient vessels support discussion of cacao cultivation and exchange, although the scale of that economy remains a research question. A modern community now overlaps the archaeological settlement.

site-0587.description: Balberta grew into a major Early Classic centre on Guatemala’s Pacific coastal plain, reaching its strongest phase around AD 200–400. Its architecture remains especially informative because extensive later construction did not cover the early monumental core. Imported green obsidian and ceramic cacao-bean effigies point to exchange with central Mexico. Cacao has been proposed as a valuable export, although trade evidence alone does not establish direct Teotihuacan control. The centre declined around AD 400 as nearby Montana rose in importance.

site-0609.description: Monte Alto belongs to the Pacific-side archaeological landscape of Guatemala. It is especially known for rounded stone sculptures conventionally called potbellies and for large carved heads. These monuments are important to discussions of early sculptural traditions in southern Mesoamerica. Their cultural attribution and relationship to neighbouring societies require care; inclusion in the MayaMap survey does not by itself establish that every monument represents a specifically Maya tradition.

site-0804.description: Salinas de los Nueve Cerros developed around an inland source of brine near the Chixoy River. Salt production is central to its archaeology, with working areas and monumental groups distributed around the salt dome and nearby ridge. Its long occupation connects resource extraction with regional exchange between the lowlands and highlands. The name refers to the Nine Hills, while the site's significance lies in the unusual availability of salt away from the coast.

sources.label: Wikipedia · Salinas de los Nueve Cerros

site-0864.description: Machaquilá stood beside a tributary of the Pasión River on routes between the Maya Mountains and western waterways. It flourished in the Late and Terminal Classic, with renewed political activity as the power of Dos Pilas diminished. Shared emblem-glyph associations suggest links with Cancuén, although the exact organisation of that relationship remains debated. Its monuments and ceremonial core preserve the history of a kingdom that gained prominence during regional political change.

site-0867.description: Ixtutz occupied the Poxte River valley in the Maya Mountains and was an important centre in the Dolores region. It competed with neighbouring kingdoms during the Late Classic while maintaining connections toward southwestern Petén, including Dos Pilas and Machaquilá. Its occupation began earlier and continued into the Terminal Classic. The site's position helps explain the interaction between local valley politics and the larger kingdoms beyond the mountains.

site-0869.description: Ixkún was a kingdom in the upper Mopan region, with a large ceremonial centre and many unrestored structures. Its exceptionally tall Stela 1 is a major surviving monument of southern Petén. The settlement occupied a route linking the Dolores valley with the Mopan drainage and nearby cities. Although its principal activity belongs to the Late Classic, archaeological evidence indicates a longer occupation extending into the Postclassic.

site-0872.description: El Chal developed in southeastern Petén with an early ceremonial group north of its later urban centre. Its long occupation extended from the Preclassic into the Postclassic, with particular importance during the Late Classic. A large quadrangular residential complex is an unusual feature among southern lowland sites. The shift in the location of principal buildings demonstrates how a city's focus could move while occupation continued in the same broader landscape.

site-0878.description: Topoxté occupies islands in Lake Yaxhá and is especially significant for the Postclassic Kowoj Maya. Earlier occupation extended back into the Preclassic, but its later temples and open halls demonstrate the continuing vitality of the Petén lakes after the decline of many Classic cities. Architecture and ceramics reveal connections with northern Yucatán, including Mayapán. Changing lake levels alter the islands’ relationship to the shore, reminding visitors that the settlement’s defensive and transport setting depended on a dynamic waterscape.

site-0881.description: Naranjo was the seat of the Sa'aal dynasty in eastern Petén and reached its greatest prominence during the Late Classic. Its centre contains triadic groups, palace compounds, ballcourts and a hieroglyphic stairway. Painted ceramics and carved monuments preserve a distinctive courtly record. The kingdom participated in alliances and wars involving Caracol, Calakmul and neighbouring cities. This history belongs to the Petén record, rather than the other places named Naranjo in the source inventory.

site-0893.description: Tikal grew from an early settlement into one of the most influential cities of the Maya lowlands. Steep temple pyramids frame the Great Plaza, while the North Acropolis preserves successive generations of ceremonial construction and royal burials. Beyond the monumental centre, residential groups, causeways and reservoirs reveal a much larger urban landscape. The city's rulers participated in far-reaching alliances and conflicts, especially its long rivalry with Calakmul. Today the forest surrounds its surviving buildings, but the archaeological remains record an intensely managed landscape of households, water storage and political power.

site-0901.description: Nakbé is an early major settlement in the Mirador Basin, south of El Mirador. Its Preclassic remains are important for understanding the emergence of large-scale Maya masonry construction. Archaeologists have investigated both ceremonial architecture and the limestone quarries that supplied it, including tools used to extract and shape building stone. Ceramic finds help trace the settlement's early development. A causeway links Nakbé with the larger neighbouring city. The combination of early buildings, material production and regional connections makes it a valuable record of how monumental urban landscapes were created long before the Classic period.

site-0903.description: Naachtún lies between the major political centres of Tikal and Calakmul in northern Petén. Unlike several nearby Preclassic centres, it continued to develop into the Classic period. Changes in its residential groups and monumental construction record shifting relationships with those larger kingdoms. Its location makes the site particularly useful for examining how a substantial local court navigated the competing networks of the central Maya lowlands.

site-0905.description: Kinal developed on a plateau above seasonal wetlands in northeastern Petén. Its approaches were strengthened with high platforms and walls during the later Classic centuries. A major building programme in the eighth century reflects the settlement's regional importance after changes at nearby Río Azul. The combination of natural slopes and constructed barriers makes it particularly useful for studying defensive planning, while its monumental remains document substantial investment in a protected urban core.

site-0907.description: Xultún contains temples, ballcourts, stelae and reservoirs in northern Petén. A painted room preserves court figures alongside calendrical calculations, offering rare evidence of the work of Maya specialists in a built setting. The images and notations connect political life with knowledge of lunar cycles. Its broader settlement and nearby quarries also record the material effort behind urban construction. Research at Xultún is closely connected with investigations of neighbouring San Bartolo.

The available record supports discussion of those monuments, but a detailed sequence of local rulers and building phases remains uncertain.

site-1167.description: El Temblor is a compact settlement southeast of Tikal, with three principal groups arranged along a north–south line. A hilltop pyramid, palatial remains, platforms and a subterranean storage chamber form part of the recorded architecture. A damaged stela connects the site to the written history of smaller Petén centres. Looting has affected both buildings and monuments, making earlier documentation especially important for understanding remains that have since been altered or removed.

site-1193.description:
Kohunlich is distinguished by the large stucco faces that flank the stairway of the Temple of the Masks. Traces of red pigment survive on figures interpreted as royal persons wearing solar attributes. Around this temple, residential, civic and religious buildings spread through the forest, making the site more than a single celebrated monument. Its modern name derives from the English expression Cohoon Ridge, referring to the area's palms. Looking from the sculpted faces to the surrounding architectural groups reveals the relationship between the display of royal authority and the spaces used by the broader community.

INAH’s guide places the civic and residential core on the higher western plain, with lower eastern ground supporting food production and water storage. The Yaxná group preserves some of the earliest monumental construction and high-status burials. Later growth produced varied neighbourhoods rather than a single compact temple precinct.

The Las Vías group yielded unfinished stone tools and flint-working debris, providing evidence of craft activity. The Pixa’an and Twenty-Seven Steps groups preserve substantial residential compounds, while the Merwin Plaza contains buildings with several forms of columns and porticoes. Later platforms and offerings among abandoned buildings indicate that parts of the settlement remained in use after its major construction projects had ceased. The celebrated stucco masks are interpreted in the guide as royal or ancestral figures bearing solar attributes, connecting rulership with sacred imagery.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History
INAH · Kohunlich archaeological guide (2019)
sources.author: INAH
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1194.description: Kaminaljuyú was a major centre in the Valley of Guatemala, with a long occupation reaching back into the Preclassic. Its buildings were largely constructed from earth and adobe, giving the surviving mounds a very different appearance from lowland limestone temples. Modern Guatemala City has absorbed much of the ancient settlement, and the archaeological park preserves only part of its former extent. Excavations, sculpture and buried structures provide evidence for its connections and changing importance. Understanding Kaminaljuyú requires looking beyond the modest visible remains to the much larger city documented through archaeological investigation.

site-1201.description: El Zotz lies west of Tikal in a landscape of cliffs, caves and seasonal wetlands. Its modern name refers to the bats associated with nearby cave systems. The Classic settlement contains temple groups and many unexcavated structures, including the prominent El Diablo complex. Its court's history intersects with the political networks of central Petén. The historical survey coordinate is retained; published locations vary, so the map point should be read as approximate.

site-1203.description: Cival was an important Preclassic centre near the Holmul River in eastern Petén. Its raised temples, ceremonial plazas and surviving stucco imagery show that elaborate monumental and religious architecture developed well before the Classic period. Research began as part of investigations of nearby Holmul before the site's earlier significance became clear. The remains help explain the deep history of urban life in a region later occupied by competing Classic kingdoms.

site-1204.description: La Sufricaya lies close to Holmul in eastern Petén. Its murals and stelae include imagery associated with central Mexican traditions, raising questions about foreign presence and political interaction during the Early Classic. Archaeologists study the site's relationship with Holmul as part of the same broader landscape. The images establish connections, but do not by themselves settle whether those contacts involved visitors, resident outsiders or a particular form of political control.

site-1205.description: Holmul occupied routes connecting inland Petén with the coast and linking northern centres with the highlands. Its strategic position drew it into the networks of Tikal and the Kaan dynasty. Early excavations were also important to archaeology itself, producing a sequence of pottery styles from successive deposits. Later work has expanded understanding of its architecture and political history. Holmul demonstrates how a comparatively modest centre could matter within several intersecting regional systems.

site-1209.description: Ek' Balam became the seat of a powerful northern Maya court during the Late Classic. Its Acropolis combines palatial rooms and funerary spaces, including the richly decorated tomb of the ruler Ukit Kan Lek Tok'. Preserved stucco turns a doorway into a monumental open mouth, surrounded by finely modelled figures. Walls, raised roads, a ballcourt and carved monuments place this extraordinary decoration within a larger urban plan. The site is particularly revealing for the craftsmanship supported by the ruling elite, from architecture and sculpture to painted surfaces and luxurious objects made for courtly use.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-1223.description: Xpuhil is one of the most recognisable expressions of Río Bec architecture. Its best-known building has three slender towers rising above a long horizontal façade, a distinctive variation on the paired towers common in the regional style. Temple-like upper forms and steep ornamental stairs emphasise height and silhouette. Earlier architecture beneath later construction also connects the settlement with traditions of the Petén. The atlas preserves the survey name Xpuhil 1 for this record; the highlighted story refers to the principal archaeological group rather than every similarly named group in the surrounding modern town.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-1224.description:
Calakmul was a powerful city whose rulers built a network of alliances across the Maya lowlands. Its rivalry with Tikal shaped the histories of many smaller kingdoms. Thousands of structures extend beyond its monumental core, showing the scale of the surrounding urban population. Structure II, an enormous pyramid enlarged through successive building phases, contains royal tombs within its accumulated architecture. Stelae and other monuments preserve traces of court life and dynastic ambition. The forest setting can make the ruins seem isolated today, although their history belongs to a densely connected political landscape.

Calakmul's buildings preserve successive construction projects inside later monuments. The INAH guide describes earlier architecture enclosed within Structure II, including monumental masks and a broad decorated frieze. Rebuilding incorporated these earlier works into a larger architectural mass, so the visible exterior represents only part of the monument's history.

The Chik Naab complex offers a different kind of evidence: paintings with a broad color palette and carefully rendered clothing survive on a buried building. Elite residences and richly furnished burials in the Great Acropolis further distinguish palace life from the public plazas. The guide emphasizes that the city's development continued after its defeat by Tikal in 695, while later offerings and incense burners indicate visits after royal power had declined. Political defeat, urban change and the end of ritual activity were separate processes.

sources.label: INAH · Calakmul archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Ramón Carrasco Vargas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1225.description: Balamkú preserves an extraordinary modelled and painted stucco frieze from an earlier palace concealed beneath a later building. The decoration combines figures and supernatural imagery in a composition interpreted as connecting different levels of the Maya cosmos. Its survival owes much to the deliberate filling and covering of the palace during rebuilding. The sculpted surface retains evidence of colour, reminding us that Maya monuments were not originally bare stone. This record appears in the source inventory as Balamku or Chunhabil; the highlighted drawing focuses on the site's surviving frieze rather than an imagined complete reconstruction.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-1226.description:
Hormiguero's Structure II combines slender ornamental towers with an enormous monster-mouth entrance. This dramatic façade brings together Río Bec and Chenes architectural elements in a single building. Other groups include temples and many structures that remain largely unexcavated. The city's principal flourishing belongs to the Late Classic, around 650–850 CE. Its buildings are especially revealing for the inventive ways regional architects combined height, horizontal mass and sculptural doorways.

Hormiguero lies near the meeting of the Río Bec and Petén architectural regions. Structure II preserves an especially elaborate south façade: a central monster-mouth entrance is flanked by tower forms and additional ornamented doorways. The building contained eight rooms in two parallel ranges. Its rear façade was comparatively plain, with a portico whose columns probably supported a perishable roof.

INAH’s guide describes an earlier building beneath this structure, demonstrating that the celebrated façade belongs to a sequence of rebuilding. In the Central Group, Structure V rises above a vaulted passage and repeats some of the larger building’s tower and mask motifs on a smaller scale. The contrast between its surviving west side and damaged east side makes the difference between preserved fabric and reconstruction particularly important.

sources.label: INAH · Hormiguero archaeological guide (1999)
sources.author: Ángeles Cantero Aguilar
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1227.description: Chicanná's buildings are celebrated for façades in which architectural doorways become the open jaws of a supernatural being. Structure II is the clearest example, with a carefully composed arrangement of eyes, teeth and other sculpted elements surrounding the entrance. Other mask panels show variations in this regional imagery. The settlement stood close to Becán, and archaeological research places it within that larger city's sphere of interaction. Its surviving palatial architecture suggests an elite community whose builders invested heavily in decoration, making the transition from an outdoor plaza to an interior room a visually charged experience.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-1228.description:
Becán's most unusual feature is the deep ditch surrounding its central precinct, the feature that inspired its modern name. The settlement began in the Middle Preclassic and later developed imposing buildings in the Río Bec architectural tradition. Imported material indicates connections with distant Teotihuacan, while its position near Chicanná and Xpuhil places it within a busy regional network. Construction and population changed considerably over its long history. The combination of a bounded monumental core, large temple structures and surrounding settlement makes Becán a particularly useful place to examine urban organisation and the control of access.

Becán’s monumental core was enclosed by a ditch and parapet, with seven crossings providing access. INAH’s guide notes that the ditch may initially have drained excess rainwater before serving defensive purposes. Most inhabitants lived outside this enclosure, so the prominent ruins represent a restricted centre within a wider settlement.

Structure VIII combines a long palace, eight rooms and tall lateral towers; an interior passage connects additional vaulted chambers. Structure X forms part of a complex of courtyards and many rooms, including a central palace with benches, niches and fittings for curtains. Successive construction concealed parts of this earlier arrangement beneath stepped platforms. At Structure IX, excavations identified multiple phases and recovered a group of ceramic vessels whose imagery and inscriptions contribute to the site’s history.

sources.label: INAH · Becán archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Antonio Benavides Castillo
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1229.description: Dzibilnocac developed in the Chenes region near modern Vicente Guerrero. Its principal palace-temple combines a long range of vaulted rooms with towers and elaborate mask decoration. A longer occupation preceded its Late Classic flourishing. The visible architecture exemplifies the region's interest in turning façades and entrances into large sculptural compositions. Much of the wider settlement remains represented by mounds, so the best-known building is only part of the ancient city.

site-1232.description:
Mayapán was a major political and cultural centre in the northern Yucatán during the Late Postclassic. Thousands of structures, most of them houses, occupied the densely settled area inside its long perimeter wall, with additional neighbourhoods outside. Its ceremonial centre combines pyramids, shrines, colonnaded halls and round buildings in closely packed spaces. The main pyramid echoes the better-known El Castillo at Chichén Itzá. Mayapán offers a different picture from the forest cities of the Classic period: its archaeology is especially useful for understanding households, craft activity and political life in the centuries before Spanish colonisation.

Mayapán's surviving paintings add an intimate counterpoint to its walls and monumental pyramid. The INAH guide describes painted niches, serpent imagery and aquatic scenes that once gave several buildings vividly colored surfaces. In the Temple of the Painted Niches, miniature temple fronts appear above serpent heads; the Fisherman's Temple includes a scene involving a person, fish and an alligator.

Another painted ensemble beside the Castillo shows richly dressed figures holding a circular solar emblem against blue. These details connect architecture with imagery also encountered in painted manuscripts and wider Mesoamerican traditions. The guide cautions against treating the famous alliance of Mayapán, Uxmal and Chichén Itzá as a straightforward contemporary federation: archaeological evidence places their principal periods of prominence at different times. The city's history requires both documentary traditions and excavation evidence.

sources.label: INAH · Mayapán archaeological guide (2019)
sources.author: Carlos Alberto Peraza Lope
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1233.description: Bonampak is best known for the paintings preserved in the three rooms of its Temple of the Murals. Their crowded scenes depict court ceremony, warfare and its aftermath, offering unusually vivid evidence of elite dress, musicians, gestures and political display. The city's history was closely tied to nearby Yaxchilán, a larger power in the Usumacinta region. The temple stands on an acropolis above the main plaza, so its intimate painted interiors form part of a broader public setting. Lacandon Maya knew and visited these ruins before they became widely known to outside researchers.

site-1234.description: Yaxchilán follows a bend of the Usumacinta River, with plazas and buildings arranged on terraces rising from the riverbank. Its carved lintels, stelae, altars and steps preserve accounts of rulers, warfare and ritual across several centuries. Structure 33, crowned by a monumental roof comb, is its most recognisable building. The site is especially important for the close integration of architectural entrances and narrative sculpture. Later Lacandon visitors continued to hold ceremonies among the ancient temples, leaving evidence that the ruins remained meaningful long after the royal court had disappeared.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-1235.description: Palenque stands where the Chiapas foothills meet the lowlands. Its architecture combines carefully proportioned rooms, elaborate roof combs and sculpted panels with a landscape threaded by streams. The Temple of the Inscriptions contains the tomb of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, linking a ruler's burial with a monumental written account. Nearby, the Palace and the temples of the Cross Group preserve remarkable reliefs and inscriptions. Together these works make the city especially valuable for understanding Maya royal history, religious imagery and the close relationship between carved texts and the buildings that carried them.

site-1433.description: La Mar occupied hills overlooking the Santo Domingo valley in Chiapas. Its fortifications controlled approaches from lower ground, and inscriptions connect its rulers with the conflicts of the Usumacinta region. During the eighth century it allied with Piedras Negras and participated in campaigns against Pomoná. The named ruler Parrot Chaak appears in that wider written record. La Mar illustrates how smaller courts took active roles in regional alliances and warfare.

site-1495.description: Xupá is a Classic centre in the Palenque region near the Chacamax River. Its temple decoration has strong affinities with Palenque's architectural and sculptural traditions. Early explorers recorded a finely incised stone panel that was subsequently removed, illustrating the importance of historical documentation for monuments no longer in place. The site was smaller than initial reports suggested, but its surviving and recorded imagery contributes to the study of Palenque's wider cultural sphere.

site-1623.description: Tenam Rosario was a substantial centre in the eastern Chiapas highlands, with important activity in the Late Classic and into the Early Postclassic. Its remains include ceremonial and residential groups, pyramids and ballcourts. Carved ballcourt markers and other stone monuments provide evidence of local religious imagery and political display. Much of the architecture remains unexcavated, so descriptions of the city depend on survey and recovered monuments as well as standing structures.

site-1721.description: Moxviquil is a smaller archaeological centre near San Cristóbal de las Casas in the Chiapas highlands. Investigations documented a main settlement and nearby burial caves. Its remains have been interpreted in relation to local administration and economic activity, broadening the picture beyond the lowland royal cities. Material recovered during twentieth-century research forms part of the historical record of archaeological work in this highland region.

site-1765.description: Chiapa de Corzo was an early regional centre near the Grijalva River. Its Formative-period platforms, plazas, offerings and elite burials reveal connections with wider Mesoamerican traditions, including Olmec imagery. Its cultural history is often discussed in relation to Mixe-Zoquean populations. This is a peripheral record in the MayaMap inventory, not a reason to label all of its remains Maya. The survey location is retained separately from that cultural distinction.

site-1946.description:
The INAH guide emphasizes Izapa’s place in the Mixe-Zoque cultural region and its connections with artistic traditions that later flourished across the Maya world. Groups of earthen mounds enclose plazas where stelae and altars were carefully positioned. Later buildings in Group F used river stones from the nearby Izapa River as facing material.

The carved monuments combine people, animals and supernatural beings in complex scenes. Some arrange imagery into celestial, earthly and underworld zones. The guide interprets Stela 5’s great tree as an axis linking those realms, while other carvings depict ritual, rulership and mythological action. These are interpretations of a distinctive sculptural tradition, not a fully deciphered written account. The setting beneath the volcanic highlands forms an important part of the site’s wider landscape.

site-2069.description: Chacchoben contains large temple platforms and pyramids in southern Quintana Roo. The settlement began before the Classic period, while much of its prominent architecture belongs to the later first millennium CE. Some buildings preserve traces of red pigment, protected during conservation. Archaeological investigation and restoration have revealed only part of the site, with additional structures remaining beneath vegetation. Its monumental groups show the scale of inland settlement behind the Caribbean coast.

site-2116.description:
Muyil, also called Chunyaxché, lies beside the lagoons of the eastern Yucatán. Its steep temple architecture has affinities with Petén traditions, while canals and coastal routes connected the settlement to exchange networks. Finds indicate occupation from the Preclassic through the late pre-Hispanic centuries. The site has also been linked with Cobá. Its combination of inland monumental buildings and access to a lagoon system helps explain the relationship between forest settlements and Caribbean trade.

Muyil comprises several architectural groups rather than a single compact monument. The INAH guide distinguishes its principal precinct, a cenote group and western remains, with local causeways connecting parts of the settlement. The buildings visible on a visit represent only a portion of the ancient community, whose location also connected it with lagoon resources and regional movement.

The Castillo combines a tall temple platform with an unusual solid circular element above the sanctuary; the guide leaves that feature's function unresolved. Traces of red and Maya blue paint recall the buildings' former appearance. Temple 8 preserves successive stairways and an inner sanctuary enclosed by later construction, with painted surfaces surviving within. Differences between earlier architecture and later East Coast forms make Muyil especially useful for following changing building traditions through time, without assuming that every visible structure belongs to the same phase.

site-2117.description: Cobá developed beside lakes in the eastern Yucatán and connected its dispersed building groups with raised stone roads called sacbeob. One exceptionally long causeway reaches west to Yaxuná, over 100 kilometres away. The Nohoch Mul group contains the city's best-known tall pyramid, while carved stelae record rulers and ceremonies. Much of the monumental construction belongs to the middle and later Classic centuries, but repair and building continued into the Postclassic. The roads are essential to reading Cobá: they reveal a city organised through movement between widely separated plazas, neighbourhoods and allied places.

site-2119.description: Xelhá was a coastal settlement and port linked to inland centres, particularly Cobá. Evidence spans the Classic and Postclassic, with many visible structures rebuilt in the later period. Its inlet supported maritime exchange and later became a landing place for Spanish expeditions. The ancient settlement should be distinguished from the modern attraction using the same name: the archaeological record concerns the buildings, inscriptions and occupation associated with the historic port.

site-2187.description: Cucá preserves a compact group of structures near Tixpéhual in northern Yucatán. The remains include a low enclosing wall and a temple mound with traces of painted decoration. A raised road crosses the settlement and has been associated with connections toward T'Hó, the ancient city beneath Mérida. The available account places the site in the Postclassic landscape, where movement between established towns was an important part of regional organisation.

site-2190.description:
Acanceh preserves major Maya monuments within a modern town southeast of Mérida. Large masks survive on an earlier stage of its pyramid, while the Palace of the Stuccos carries elaborate architectural decoration. These buildings are part of a much larger ancient settlement beneath the present streets. Their sculptural detail and evidence of connections beyond the northern lowlands make Acanceh an important example of continuity and transformation in an inhabited archaeological landscape.

INAH’s guide describes an ancient settlement extending across roughly three square kilometres beneath and around the modern town. Its main pyramid was originally decorated with eight large stucco masks beside four stairways. Early photographs and surviving fragments helped researchers document decoration that had already disappeared from part of the building by the 1930s. The masks made sacred imagery visible in a public ceremonial setting.

The Palace of the Stuccoes stands on a substantial platform. Its small rooms and earlier construction suggest ritual use, while later buildings on the platform may have served administrative purposes. The painted frieze combines stylized mammals, birds and other supernatural figures within stepped frames; ochre, green and red were prominent colours. The guide interprets this imagery in relation to the celestial realm and the ruling lineage, while treating the precise identities of the figures as uncertain.

site-2467.description: Xkipché is a Puuc-region settlement south of Uxmal whose best-known structure is a substantial two-storey palace. Its rooms and façades form part of a broader group of Classic-period buildings. Burials and human remains have also been studied for evidence of differences within the community. Early documentation by Teobert Maler is significant because later research had to relocate and reassess structures that had received little attention for many years.

site-2493.description: Kiuic is a Puuc settlement with evidence of occupation reaching back to around 800 BC and a major architectural flowering in the Late Classic period. Palaces, pyramidal platforms and courtyards form groups including Yaxché, Chulul and Kuche. Investigations of the Yaxché plazas have helped establish the community’s long sequence before its later abandonment. Its relatively well-preserved residential and ceremonial remains make Kiuic valuable for examining daily life and settlement change alongside the region’s more famous monumental centres.

site-2695.description: Actun Tunichil Muknal preserves a Maya ceremonial landscape inside a river cave in Belize’s Cayo District. Pottery, stone objects and human remains occur in upper chambers, where mineral deposits have encrusted many ancient offerings. Some vessels were deliberately perforated, helping archaeologists distinguish ritual deposits from ordinary household refuse. The cave shows how Maya sacred places extended beyond built temples into subterranean spaces shaped by water and limestone. Its fragile deposits require careful conservation.

site-2701.description: This Belizean survey record relates to El Pilar, the extensive Maya centre that crosses the modern Belize–Guatemala border. Its numerous plazas and surrounding settlement have been studied together with agricultural land and forest resources. Work led by Anabel Ford emphasises the relationship between households and the managed landscape. The atlas also retains separate Guatemalan records for this border area; their different survey coordinates should not be mistaken for precise limits of independent cities.

site-2707.description: Yo'okop, also written Okop, occupies the Cochuah region of central Quintana Roo beside a shallow lake. Ceramics and architecture indicate a long occupation from the Formative through the Postclassic. Its large, partly vegetation-covered structures reveal a more substantial urban centre than its limited early investigation suggested. Archaeological work here helps fill the geographic gap between the better-known northern cities and the monumental centres farther south.

site-2737.description:
Pomoná occupied a strategic setting between the coastal plain and routes along the Usumacinta. The INAH guide presents control of movement through this landscape as a possible reason for rivalry involving Palenque and Piedras Negras. Captives associated with Pomoná appear on Piedras Negras Stela 12, placing the city within documented regional conflict.

The settlement was dispersed among six major architectural groups. Builders transported limestone from the nearby foothills to create platforms and sculpted monuments. In Group I, a large open plaza is framed by higher structures on the north and west and lower platforms on the east. Building 3 is notable for stairway slabs bearing solar imagery. Building 1 retains a fragmentary circular altar in front of its main stairway. These surviving details connect the city's political history with the organization of its public spaces.

sources.label: INAH · Pomoná archaeological guide (2017)
sources.author: Ito J. Kato Vidal

site-2746.description: This Guatemalan record marks the El Pilar archaeological landscape near the Belize border. The ancient centre contains many plazas and substantial buildings within a broader area of settlement and farmland. Its modern archaeological reserve spans both countries, reflecting a landscape that predates the international boundary. Separate source records preserve different surveyed positions around the complex. The account concerns that shared centre, while this particular map marker retains the original Petén coordinate and bibliography.

site-2810.description:
Tenam Puente's Acropolis was created by repeatedly leveling and terracing a hill. Its different elevations directed movement between plazas and more restricted spaces. The INAH guide distinguishes this highland building tradition from lowland Maya architecture: corbelled stone vaults were not used here, and several buildings have substantial sloping retaining walls.

Three ballcourts show the importance of ritual gatherings. The largest occupies an open plaza below the Acropolis, where a considerable audience could assemble. Burials placed within Building 7 included objects from distant regions, while a tomb in Building 21 contained jadeite, marine shells and a carved bone serpent. These finds connect the hilltop community with wider exchange networks. Modeled stucco on Building 29 included Venus and death-related imagery, adding another layer to the way architecture framed ritual experience.

site-2816.description:
Lagartero's inhabitants adapted an island and wetland landscape. The main civic and ceremonial precinct occupies Limonal Island, while smaller remains around the marsh reflect a wider settlement. Fishing and hunting supplemented maize and cotton farming; imported obsidian and other goods connected the community with distant regions.

The INAH guide describes terraced buildings arranged around plazas and smaller courtyards, together with a ballcourt. On two pyramids, recessed forms resemble an inverted T, a motif interpreted by some researchers as a reference to wind. The Guajil Pyramid has a broad stairway rising through its stepped platform to the remains of a temple. Excavated figurines preserve unusually specific details of clothing and headdresses, while broken pottery and animal remains provide evidence for ceremonial deposits. These finds bring household life, exchange and ritual into the history of the same marshland community.

sources.label: INAH · Lagartero archaeological guide (2018)

site-2878.description: Holtun, also recorded as La Máquina, occupies a limestone ridge in eastern Petén. Monumental stucco masks, a triadic acropolis and an E-Group complex reveal substantial Preclassic ceremonial investment. Residential construction and rebuilding continued into the Classic period. Numerous chultuns cut into the bedrock add evidence for how inhabitants adapted the ridge to settlement needs. Reports of looting prompted official investigation in 1994; subsequent surveys and excavations have greatly expanded the mapped settlement beyond the first recorded buildings.

site-2908.description: La Joyanca lies south of the San Pedro Mártir River in northwestern Petén. It experienced a long occupation, with substantial population growth and construction during the Late Classic. Archaeological work on its ceremonial and residential groups has contributed to understanding settlement organisation in this part of the lowlands. Its investigation also connects with studies at Zapote Bobal and Pajaral, allowing local histories to be considered together rather than only through the larger eastern kingdoms.

site-3327.description: Sacul was a Classic Maya kingdom in the hilly upper Mopan region of southeastern Petén. Its monuments preserve evidence of local rulers and interaction with neighbouring kingdoms. Ceremonial buildings and plazas occupy the valley landscape, while routes through the Maya Mountains connected the community to other centres. Its political history is best understood alongside Ixkún and Ixtontón, rather than as an isolated collection of mounds.

site-3353.description: Dos Pilas was founded by a branch of Tikal's dynasty, then became aligned with Tikal's great rival Calakmul. Its rulers retained the same emblem associated with Tikal, making the city a vivid example of divided dynastic identity. Hieroglyphic stairways preserve a detailed sequence of conflicts and political events. Dos Pilas and Aguateca eventually served as twin centres of a kingdom in the Petexbatún region. The city's comparatively short history illuminates the pressures of Late Classic warfare, while its surviving monuments allow those wider rivalries to be followed through the actions of particular rulers.

site-3354.description: Arroyo de Piedra was an established Classic centre before the foundation of nearby Dos Pilas. Its architecture and inscriptions connect it closely with Tamarindito, with which it formed an earlier political unit. The rise of Dos Pilas reduced its independent standing. Its subsequent decline belongs to the wider disruption of the Petexbatún region, making the site useful for understanding the histories of communities absorbed by expanding kingdoms.

site-3355.description: Tamarindito was an established centre in the Petexbatún region before the rise of Dos Pilas. Its hilltop position overlooks lakes and surrounding routes. Inscriptions document a local dynasty, while an excavated royal tomb contained rich offerings. After subordination to Dos Pilas, Tamarindito participated in its defeat during the eighth century. The settlement's subsequent decline shows that victory over an overlord did not prevent the wider political and demographic disruption of the region.

site-3543.description: El Meco was a coastal settlement north of modern Cancún that became important in Postclassic maritime exchange. Its principal pyramid, known as El Castillo, overlooks a ceremonial plaza with smaller shrines and platforms. The position facing the sea connects its architecture with the movement of people and goods along the coast. Earlier occupation preceded its later expansion, placing the site within the changing network of northern Quintana Roo ports.

site-3555.description:
Labná's freestanding decorated arch is one of the most distinctive surviving monuments of the Puuc region. Its corbelled opening frames passage between architectural spaces, while finely worked ornament covers the upper façade. The nearby Palace and the temple called El Mirador show the same attention to surface and silhouette. Settlement began earlier, but the city's main flowering came around 800–1000 CE. Labná was a medium-sized community, possibly linked to a larger regional capital; the elaborate surviving buildings show that exceptional craftsmanship was not confined to the largest Maya cities.

Labná’s central buildings occupy a valley surrounded by residential hills. INAH’s guide distinguishes earlier construction around the southern ceremonial area from later enlargement of the Palace complex. The Palace grew through several stages, with earlier rooms and patios incorporated into a much larger platform and rows of vaulted chambers. Unfinished rooms in its northeastern sector preserve evidence that the final project was never completed.

A relief associated with Room 19 contains a date corresponding to AD 862; the guide suggests it may commemorate the dedication of a throne room. A causeway linked the Palace with the sacred precinct near the Mirador and Arch. The buildings also show changes within Puuc architecture, from relatively plain walls and stucco roof decoration to elaborate stone mosaics. Numerous underground cisterns supplied stored rainwater within the settlement.

site-3562.description: Ixtontón was a major kingdom in the upper Mopan valley near modern Dolores. Its acropolis occupies a modified limestone hill, with principal buildings arranged around two plazas. The settlement has a long sequence from the Late Preclassic through the Terminal Classic, with some later activity. Its position among rivers, savanna and hill country supported regional connections. Archaeological comparison with Ixkún and Ixtutz helps reconstruct the changing political geography of southeastern Petén.

site-3567.description: Ixlú stands between Lakes Petén Itzá and Salpetén, where river access made it an important port. Its long occupation culminated in a substantial Postclassic settlement associated with the Kowoj region. Earlier ballcourts, sculpted monuments and a twin-pyramid complex preserve a different layer of Classic-period history. The Temple of the Hidden Jars takes its name from covered vessels placed in concealed niches. Together, these remains show that the Petén lakes continued supporting active communities long after many Classic royal centres declined.

site-3568.description: Uaxactún lies north of Tikal and has played a major role in the study of early Maya architecture. Investigations of its Group E gave the name E-Group to a widespread arrangement of ceremonial buildings often discussed in relation to solar observation. Earlier structures, including a mask-decorated platform, survived beneath later construction. Excavations also helped establish sequences of Maya pottery and building phases. Its modern name was coined by Sylvanus Morley after an early dated inscription. The site's importance therefore lies both in its ancient history and in the development of archaeological understanding of the Maya lowlands.

site-3569.description: Tulum occupies a limestone cliff above the Caribbean, within a compact settlement enclosed by walls on its landward sides. Most surviving buildings belong to the Late Postclassic, when coastal exchange connected communities around the Yucatán Peninsula. El Castillo, the Temple of the Frescoes and smaller shrines illustrate the region's comparatively low, compact temple architecture. Earlier finds indicate a longer history than the standing buildings alone suggest. Its position beside the sea is central to understanding the site: this was part of an inhabited trading coast, with religious buildings and routes linking it to inland Maya centres.

site-3756.description: Dzibilchaltún developed around an accessible water source, the Xlacah cenote, north of modern Mérida. Its surviving plazas and paved causeways connect structures from different phases of a long occupation. The Temple of the Seven Dolls takes its modern name from small ceramic figures found during excavation; its opposing doorways create the celebrated sunrise view. Elsewhere, carved stelae, long public buildings and an open colonial chapel reveal changes in the use of the same landscape. The cenote and roads are as important to understanding this settlement as its compact, distinctive temple.

site-3757.description: Baking Pot occupies the southern side of the Belize River valley. Research has examined residential groups, stone-tool production and the agricultural economy as well as the ceremonial centre. Some surrounding households remained occupied into the Postclassic, after activity in the monumental core diminished. This uneven pattern provides evidence for community continuity beyond the decline of royal institutions, rather than a single moment when the whole settlement was abandoned.

site-3928.description:
Mitla is a Zapotec city in Oaxaca, retained here as part of the original atlas's broader Mesoamerican inventory. Its principal later palaces developed after Monte Albán's decline. Five monumental groups preserve different layouts: some arrange platforms around open plazas, while others organize residential and administrative rooms around enclosed courtyards.

The Hall of the Columns contains large monolithic supports that once carried its roof. Nearby rooms display mosaics assembled from finely cut stones into intricate geometric panels; the individual pieces of this decorative work fit together without mortar. Cross-shaped tombs beneath the southern complex continue the architectural decoration below ground. The Church Group also preserves traces of manuscript-like mural painting and the later insertion of the Church of Saint Paul. Together, the buildings record a specifically Zapotec architectural tradition and the transformation of an inhabited place through the colonial period.

site-4309.description: Casa Blanca is part of the Chalchuapa archaeological zone, near Tazumal in western El Salvador. Several structures stand on a broad artificial platform whose construction began in the Late Preclassic. Occupation and ceremonial use changed over time, including later reuse for burials and pilgrimage. The archaeological park preserves only part of the larger complex. Its modern name derives from the coffee estate that occupied the land.

site-4358.description: El Puente was a Maya centre in the Florida valley of northwestern Honduras. Its ceremonial and residential remains include pyramids, terraces and plazas, with a settlement history extending through the Classic period. Archaeological research places it within the wider political landscape of Copán and neighbouring communities. The site broadens the atlas beyond the great Copán centre, showing the smaller courts and settlements that occupied the southeastern edge of the Maya world.

site-4769.description:
Izamal's ancient monumental platforms remain embedded in a living town. The enormous Kinich Kak Moo complex is the most conspicuous survivor, but several other structures preserve the scale of the earlier city. Builders here developed a distinctive use of very large stone blocks, broad stairs and rounded or recessed corners. Roads connected Izamal with neighbouring centres, including Aké, reflecting its regional importance. Religious traditions associated the place with Zamná and solar worship. Reading Izamal requires looking across modern streets as well as individual ruins, because the ancient urban landscape was transformed rather than simply abandoned.

Izamal’s ancient settlement extended beyond the modern town. INAH’s guide describes a major plaza framed by monumental religious buildings and a causeway network reaching surrounding communities. Residential remains along the road to Aké show that movement between centres also passed through inhabited landscapes.

The Itzamatul platform preserves several construction stages, with an earlier stepped building eventually enclosed inside a much larger base. At Kabul, nineteenth-century drawings and investigations recorded stucco decoration that no longer survives. Other groups, including Habuc and Chaltunha, preserve different parts of the city’s architectural history. The Franciscan monastery was erected over another major pre-Hispanic platform, transforming the southern edge of the ancient plaza. Izamal therefore offers a layered urban landscape in which later construction both damaged and incorporated earlier monuments.

site-4931.description:
Loltún is a cave system with evidence of human activity extending far earlier than the monumental Maya cities. Paintings, hand images, tools and pottery document different uses of its chambers, while extinct-animal remains belong to a deeper environmental history. Maya communities used the cave for activities including shelter and clay extraction. Its archaeology therefore spans several kinds of evidence that should not all be assigned to one period or function.

Loltún preserves evidence of uses that extend well beyond a single Maya building period. Its chambers sheltered early inhabitants of the peninsula and later became settings for ritual activity. Carved water-catching basins, altered rock surfaces and an altar show how people adapted the natural cave rather than constructing a conventional temple precinct.

At the Nahkab entrance, a relief depicts a richly dressed standing figure with a spear and elaborate headdress. Elsewhere, painted hands, animals, human figures and stepped designs survive on the rock. These traces belong to different episodes of use; they should not be read as one contemporary decorative program. The INAH guide also describes barriers associated with the nineteenth-century Caste War, a reminder that the cave's history continued long after the ancient cities changed.

site-4932.description: Copán flourished in a fertile valley near the southeastern edge of the Maya world. Its sculptors gave rulers remarkably three-dimensional form on stelae, surrounding their bodies with elaborate costumes and symbolic imagery. The Acropolis grew through repeated construction, preserving earlier buildings beneath later ones. The Hieroglyphic Stairway records an extensive dynastic narrative, while plazas, altars and ballcourt monuments connect royal history with public ceremony. Copán is especially distinctive for the density and quality of its sculpture: individual carved surfaces reward as much attention as the larger arrangement of temples and palaces.

site-4933.description: Quiriguá stood near important routes through the lower Motagua valley. Its history was closely linked to Copán until the ruler K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat defeated and captured Copán's king in 738 CE. The city's subsequent independence was expressed through an extraordinary programme of carved monuments. Tall sandstone stelae and immense sculpted boulders carry rulers, supernatural forms and hieroglyphic texts in dense compositions. The surrounding architecture is comparatively modest, making the sculpture especially prominent. Quiriguá shows how a relatively small urban centre could use monuments to announce a major change in political standing.

site-4935.description:
Kabah's palatial groups occupy raised ground in the Puuc region. The East Group served as a residence for the ruling lineage and a setting for civic and religious activity. Its buildings enclose plazas and contain numerous vaulted rooms, indicating a substantial administrative as well as ceremonial role. The Codz Poop is famous for its repeated sculpted masks, while the nearby two-storey Palace uses a more restrained arrangement of small columns and plain panels. These different treatments make the site a rich study in how Puuc architects varied decoration within a closely related group of buildings.

Kabah’s main architectural groups occupy raised parts of the terrain, with large platforms organizing plazas and controlling access between public and more restricted spaces. INAH’s guide links the Eastern Group with both royal residence and civic or religious activity during the city’s principal flowering.

The Codz Poop was altered over time: a later wing added rooms and imagery that included human figures and latticework associated with political authority. This has supported an interpretation of part of the building as a council house. In the plaza, a comparatively small altar bears inscriptions on four sides. Its damage complicates reading the original text, but surviving signs provide evidence for connections with Uxmal. The guide also records a long causeway between the two cities, placing Kabah within a broader Puuc network.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History
INAH · Kabah archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4936.description: Uxmal is a major expression of Puuc architecture, a regional tradition distinguished by smooth lower walls and richly patterned upper façades. Stone mosaics, geometric bands and long-nosed masks cover buildings arranged across the area's low hills. The unusual rounded base of the Pyramid of the Magician contrasts with the long horizontal lines of the Governor's Palace and the enclosed spaces of the Nunnery Quadrangle. Its principal monuments belong to the later Classic centuries. Their placement and decoration show that the city's builders considered the whole ceremonial landscape, as well as the details of each façade.

site-4937.description:
Sayil grew in a valley with land suitable for agriculture during the later Classic centuries. Its Grand Palace, also called the North Palace, presents a long, carefully ordered façade built through successive phases. Rows of openings, columns and decorated upper walls make it an important example of Puuc architecture. The wider settlement extended well beyond the palace, tying elite residences to farming land and systems for obtaining water. The source atlas places this record in Campeche; the archaeological site is in modern Yucatán, a distinction retained here without silently altering the original survey fields.

Sayil's layout joins monumental architecture with productive land. The INAH guide describes major stone building groups linked along a roughly north–south axis, with houses and cultivated plots between them. Fertile valley soils helped shape settlement choices despite the scarcity of accessible water; nearby Chaak Cave was one important water source.

The North Palace grew through several construction phases, but repeating columns, entrances and decorative forms gave the finished facade a coherent rhythm. Its functions extended beyond ceremony: a kitchen identified in the northwest part supports residential use alongside political and administrative activity. Sculpted monuments suggest rulers, while other archaeological evidence points to power shared among important lineages. This combination of palace design, dispersed housing and cultivation makes the city more complex than a single royal residence surrounded by empty jungle.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History
INAH · Sayil archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4938.description: Chunchucmil was a densely occupied city in western Yucatán whose remains differ from centres dominated by royal stelae. Its residential organisation and relative scarcity of dynastic monuments have encouraged interpretations emphasising commerce and multiple powerful lineages. Located between the Gulf Coast and inland settlements, it was well placed for exchange. Survey of households and routes is especially important here, where urban significance is less obvious from monumental sculpture alone.

site-4942.description: Piedras Negras was a major kingdom on the eastern bank of the Usumacinta River. Its buildings occupy a series of hills and plazas within a heavily forested landscape. The site is especially significant for finely carved monuments that connect royal portraits with dates and events. These inscriptions helped researchers recognise the historical and dynastic content of Maya writing. The city participated in shifting relationships with other river kingdoms, including Yaxchilán. Its archaeological record combines an imposing architectural setting with unusually detailed evidence for the lives and political ambitions of individual rulers.

site-4943.description: Lamanai stands beside the New River Lagoon and preserves an exceptionally long sequence of occupation, extending from early Maya settlement into the colonial period. The High Temple, Mask Temple and Jaguar Temple form the best-known monumental groups, but the site's later history is equally significant. Spanish churches and evidence of resistance document encounters that followed the pre-Hispanic centuries. Copper objects and traces of their manufacture illuminate Postclassic exchange and technology. Lamanai therefore offers a history of adaptation and continuity alongside its temple architecture, with the lagoon providing a persistent connection through a changing cultural landscape.

site-4944.description:
La Venta is an Olmec centre included in the source atlas’s wider regional inventory. Its main occupation lasted approximately 1200–400 BC. Civic and ceremonial buildings occupied a natural rise above flood-prone ground, while surrounding households combined farming with the use of forest and aquatic resources. Monumental stone had to be brought from beyond the local area.

INAH’s guide describes Complex A’s carefully arranged courtyards, basalt columns, burials and extraordinary buried offerings. Some deposits contained mosaics assembled from hundreds of greenstone blocks; Offering 4 arranged sixteen small figures in a semicircle. Their precise meanings remain debated. Stone-lined channels at the Stirling Acropolis add evidence for water management. Many original sculptures were moved to museums during twentieth-century development, so some monuments displayed at the archaeological site are replicas rather than the excavated originals.

sources.label: INAH · La Venta archaeological guide (2000)
sources.author: Rebecca Bell González Lauck
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4945.description: Dzibanché was an early seat of the Kaan, or Snake, dynasty, whose later history is closely associated with Calakmul. Its extensive settlement includes several monumental groups linked by raised roads, among them the main Dzibanché group and the large Kinichná complex. Palaces, pyramids and royal burials reveal a court with influence beyond southern Quintana Roo. The Temple of the Lintels gives a distinctive focus to the standing architecture. The site's importance lies in both its scale and its place in the changing geography of Maya dynastic power, before and after part of the lineage established itself at Calakmul.

site-4948.description: Edzná's Great Acropolis is dominated by the Building of the Five Storeys, whose western face contains vaulted rooms on successive levels. A broad stairway leads upward through this unusually inhabited-looking pyramid façade. The structure was rebuilt over time, and reused blocks bearing hieroglyphs preserve names and titles associated with the city's rulers. Research has identified a sequence of governors that includes a woman. The monument's changing architectural forms reveal several phases of design rather than one unified construction, making Edzná a striking place to study how Maya builders transformed and reused earlier structures.

sources.label: INAH · National Institute of Anthropology and History

site-4949.description: Chichén Itzá developed into a major centre of the northern Yucatán, bringing together Maya building traditions and influences from central Mexico. El Castillo dominates a ceremonial landscape that also includes the Great Ball Court, the Temple of the Warriors and the rounded building known as El Caracol. These monuments show how architecture, sculpture and public space worked together to express religious and political authority. The city's different building groups preserve changes over many centuries, rather than a single moment in Maya history. Its surviving stone reliefs are as revealing as its monumental skyline.

site-4950.description: Caracol developed on the Vaca Plateau in the foothills of the Maya Mountains. Archaeological survey revealed a far larger and more influential city than early assessments had suggested, with settlement extending across a broad managed landscape. Its monumental centre includes Caana, a high architectural complex combining temples and palatial spaces. Roads and agricultural terraces connect the story of the royal centre to that of surrounding households. Caracol was deeply involved in the rivalries of the Classic lowlands, including conflicts with Tikal. Its scale makes the relationship between urban life, food production and regional politics particularly clear.

site-4951.description: Comalcalco is exceptional among major Maya cities for its extensive use of fired bricks in monumental construction. In the alluvial lowlands of Tabasco, this material offered an alternative to the limestone masonry familiar elsewhere. The ancient settlement, associated with the name Joy Chan, occupied a strategic position in riverine exchange between the Gulf Coast and inland regions. Archaeological finds also identify substantial production of clay figurines, with moulds and workshop debris revealing specialised craft activity. Its temples and stucco decoration connect a distinctive local material tradition with the wider architectural language of the Maya world.

site-4953.description: Xunantunich's monumental centre rises above the Mopan valley in western Belize. El Castillo dominates a sequence of plazas surrounded by temples and palaces, while surviving stucco decoration adds a rich symbolic layer to the building. The settlement expanded substantially in the seventh century as its connections with Naranjo strengthened. Archaeological surveys also document the farming communities that supported the urban centre. Its history includes disruption and renewed growth, illustrating how the fortunes of a smaller kingdom could change within wider political networks. This entry refers to the Belizean site, not the similarly named survey record in Yucatán.

site-4954.description: Altun Ha developed on Belize's coastal plain, inland from the Caribbean. Its main ceremonial precinct is organised around two principal groups, with the Temple of the Masonry Altars forming the most recognisable landmark. Reservoirs and raised paths helped people navigate and obtain water in a landscape that included swampy ground. Excavations by the Royal Ontario Museum documented a long occupation, with the city reaching its greatest extent during the Classic period. The combination of monumental buildings, residential areas and water infrastructure reveals how this community supported urban life close to the coast.

site-4955.description:
Aké's best-known monument is a broad raised platform topped by rows of substantial stone columns. Its stairs use unusually large, flat slabs, giving the approach a different rhythm from the narrow steps of many Maya pyramids. This megalithic building tradition links the site with other northern centres, especially Izamal, to which a raised causeway once led. Two enclosing walls define parts of the settlement. The ruins also lie within a later henequen estate, placing the ancient ceremonial buildings alongside evidence of a much more recent phase of land use.

INAH’s guide distinguishes several building phases within the enormous Building of the Pilasters. Its upper platform carried 35 stone supports, assembled from large blocks and weathered into column-like forms. Later occupants built small rooms over part of this space, reusing or removing some supports. These changes show how monumental places acquired different functions over time.

The guide also describes Aké’s settlement beyond the central plaza: modest room foundations contrast with residences on raised stone platforms. An approximately 32-kilometre causeway connected Aké with Izamal, while other causeways linked groups within the city. Part of the long road was later covered by a surrounding wall. That sequence raises questions about changing regional relationships, although the exact political events behind it remain interpretations rather than established facts.

site-4957.description: San Gervasio is a major settlement in the interior of Cozumel. Its location over a dependable groundwater source helped sustain occupation, and its buildings expanded through the Classic and Postclassic periods. The island was an important destination for pilgrimage associated with Ix Chel, alongside its role in Caribbean exchange. Connected architectural groups preserve civic, residential and religious spaces, placing the site within both the island's local history and the wider coastal Maya world.

site-4958.description: Chinkultic lies in the lake country of eastern Chiapas. Its temples, ballcourt and carved stelae document a Classic-period court with a strong emphasis on rulers presented as warriors. Inscriptions span the later first millennium, while occupation continued into the Postclassic. The site's imagery shares elements with other Usumacinta-region centres but also has distinctive local treatments. Its monuments therefore provide evidence for both regional artistic exchange and a particular royal identity.

site-4962.description: Nadzca'an contains several architectural groups on a raised plateau northeast of Balamkú. Its buildings show changes from Petén-related forms toward Río Bec architecture over a long occupation. Stelae include a reference to Calakmul's emblem, providing evidence of wider political connections. Plazas, a ballcourt and monumental structures make it a substantial Classic centre. The separate groups reveal a dispersed urban arrangement rather than a single compact temple precinct.

site-4964.description: El Mirador demonstrates the enormous scale of Maya urban construction centuries before the best-known Classic kingdoms reached their height. Its monumental complexes include La Danta, a vast accumulation of platforms and temples, along with other groups arranged in triadic forms. Raised causeways connected the city with neighbouring settlements in northern Petén. Much of this architecture remains covered by forest, which can conceal the extent of the built landscape. Archaeological investigation showed that the largest construction belonged to the Preclassic, reshaping earlier assumptions about when complex Maya cities and large ceremonial centres developed.

During the Late Preclassic, residents transformed an earlier village into a monumental centre with temples and plazas. Canals and raised fields record investment in the surrounding landscape. The combination of waterfront location and early ceremonial architecture makes Cerros important for studying the growth of Maya kingship.
