site-4980.description: Aguateca occupies a limestone bluff above the Petexbatún landscape, with a dramatic chasm and defensive walls shaping access to the city. It shared a ruling dynasty with nearby Dos Pilas. An attack and fire brought a rapid end to occupation in the central area, leaving objects on the floors of elite residences. These unusually informative deposits reveal household activities and the production of crafted goods, as well as courtly life. The Palace Group and Main Plaza were connected by a causeway. Aguateca is especially valuable for the evidence of everyday work preserved alongside the remains of political conflict.

site-4981.description:
Tres Zapotes belongs to the Olmec and Epi-Olmec world of Veracruz, rather than being a Maya city. The original atlas includes it within its wider regional coverage. Its major mound groups occupy an alluvial plain and natural terraces near a stream, with separate plazas distributed across the settlement.

The INAH guide emphasizes the site's long sequence through the transition from Olmec traditions into later regional developments. Stela C preserves an early Long Count calendar inscription, while colossal heads and other carved monuments document public imagery and authority. Investigations of pottery established a lengthy regional chronology. Volcanic deposits also affected the settlement landscape, and researchers have considered whether eruptions helped shift occupation toward higher terraces. The earth mounds, sculpture and environmental evidence therefore tell complementary parts of the story, rather than reducing the site to its famous heads.

site-4985.description: Ceibal, also written Seibal or El Ceibal, occupies bluffs above the Pasión River. Its history includes an early flourishing, periods of decline and a remarkable revival near the end of the Classic period. After earlier subordination to Dos Pilas, a new elite established itself in the ninth century and commissioned monuments when many neighbouring courts had already ceased to do so. The late stelae combine local traditions with wider artistic influences. This uneven history makes Ceibal especially important for understanding how individual Maya communities responded differently to the political disruptions affecting the southern lowlands.

site-4986.description:

site-4987.description: Nohmul preserves evidence of several phases of occupation in northern Belize, including renewed construction after an earlier decline. Later buildings show forms associated with northern Yucatán, suggesting changing regional connections. Its position near the Hondo River gave it access to important routes. Much of the principal pyramid was destroyed during road-material extraction in 2013, a major loss of archaeological fabric. The remaining record includes the wider settlement as well as the damaged monument.

site-4988.description: Cuello records an early farming community in northern Belize. Low plastered platforms supported houses of perishable materials arranged around patios, with burials associated with domestic spaces. An early steam bath and imported obsidian show that ritual practice and wider exchange were present at a comparatively modest settlement. Revised dating places its early occupation around 1200 BCE. The site is valuable for everyday village life, rather than only the histories of later royal cities.

site-4989.description: Cahal Pech occupies a hill above San Ignacio near the meeting of the Macal and Mopan river systems. Its compact palatial centre contains courts, vaulted rooms and temples associated with an elite household. Beneath the later architecture, early pottery and occupation deposits extend the site's history back to around 1200 BCE, making it especially important for research on the beginnings of settled life in western Belize. The contrast between the intimate surviving courtyards and this deep occupational sequence is part of its appeal: a relatively small monumental core preserves evidence spanning many centuries.

site-4991.description: Nim Li Punit takes its modern name, meaning Big Hat, from an elaborate headdress depicted on one of its carved stelae. The settlement occupies the foothills of the Maya Mountains in southern Belize, between upland terrain and the coastal lowlands. Its buildings gather around three plazas, with stone monuments providing the most distinctive evidence of royal display. Local sandstone supplied material for architecture and sculpture. Fertile soils and regional exchange helped support the community. The site rewards attention to the carved figures and texts as well as the relationship of its relatively low platforms to their landscape.

site-4992.description: Uxbenká was an early political centre in southern Belize. Its public buildings occupy modified hilltops, with residential groups dispersed across the surrounding terrain. Carved stelae preserve dates and traces of royal history despite considerable weathering. Survey and landscape research connect the monumental centre with its households and farming areas. Comparison with Nim Li Punit and Lubaantún shows that southern Belize contained several distinct communities with different histories of growth.

site-4993.description: Iximché was founded as the capital of the Kaqchikel kingdom after a break with the K'iche'. Its ridge-top setting, bordered by ravines, offered natural protection. Temple pyramids, palaces and ballcourts were arranged around a series of plazas associated with the ruling lineages. In the early sixteenth century the Kaqchikel initially allied with Spanish forces, but relations deteriorated as colonial demands grew. The city's short, consequential history links the archaeology of the highlands to written accounts of conquest and resistance. Its relatively low surviving buildings reveal a different urban form from the towering temples of Petén.

site-4994.description: Q'umarkaj, also called Utatlán or Gumarcaj, was the Late Postclassic capital of the K'iche' kingdom. Temples dedicated to important patron deities, palaces and a ballcourt were arranged around its main plaza. Written accounts complement the archaeology of this powerful highland centre at the time of Spanish invasion. Stone removal has greatly altered the surviving buildings, so the low remains do not convey the original scale of its political and ceremonial architecture.

site-4995.description: Zaculeu was the capital of a Mam kingdom in the western Guatemalan highlands and later came under K'iche' influence. Its plazas bring together temple pyramids, palaces and a ballcourt, with architectural features reflecting these overlapping histories. In 1525 its defenders endured a prolonged Spanish siege before surrendering. The bright, smooth appearance of many buildings today also reflects extensive restoration in the 1940s. That distinction matters when viewing the ruins: the surviving layout preserves an ancient political and ceremonial centre, while the visible surfaces include a substantial modern interpretation of its architecture.

site-4997.description: El Baúl belongs to the Cotzumalhuapa archaeological landscape together with Bilbao and El Castillo. Raised roads connected its monumental groups, including a route across the Santiago River gorge. Obsidian workshop debris provides evidence of specialised stone-tool production, while volcanic deposits record the influence of nearby Fuego. Its inclusion in this atlas reflects the broader Mesoamerican survey area; cultural identity should not be inferred simply from the map's Maya title.

site-4998.description: Cihuatán was a large Early Postclassic city in central El Salvador. Its extensive settlement and ceremonial areas belong to the period following major changes in neighbouring Classic centres. Excavated burnt deposits and abandoned possessions indicate a destructive fire associated with a violent end. The identity of its ruling population remains uncertain. Its presence in the source atlas should not be treated as a definitive cultural classification of the entire city as Maya.

site-4999.description: San Andrés was a major political and ceremonial centre in the Zapotitán valley during the Late Classic. An acropolis joined pyramids with spaces associated with the ruling elite, while the northern area included the large structure called La Campana. Earlier occupation and later rebuilding reflect a landscape repeatedly affected by volcanic activity. The archaeological account concerns the Salvadoran centre; other survey records called San Andrés remain separate.

site-5000.description: Joya de Cerén preserves a farming village rapidly buried by volcanic ash around 600 CE. Houses, storage spaces, working areas and plant remains offer unusually detailed evidence of daily life outside a royal court. The material was left in place as people departed, allowing archaeologists to study household activities and cultivation together. Recorded simply as Ceren in the source inventory, it is one of the most informative sites for the lives of ordinary Maya communities.

site-5001.description: Tazumal forms part of the larger archaeological landscape of Chalchuapa in western El Salvador. Its principal pyramid, Structure B1-1, grew through successive construction phases on a broad basal platform. Earlier temples and side platforms were incorporated into later enlargements, so the visible monument contains a history of rebuilding within it. Nearby structures include the Temple of the Columns and a smaller pyramid with talud-tablero forms. Finds such as green obsidian point to wider Mesoamerican connections. Tazumal is a valuable southern counterpart to the northern Maya cities, showing how local building traditions participated in broader networks.

site-5004.description:
Hochob occupies a hill whose summit was levelled to create a setting for plazas and buildings. Its richly decorated façades are characteristic of the Chenes region: carefully fitted blocks combine into enormous faces, with doorways occupying the open mouths. The Main Palace is the most recognisable example of this sculptural approach to architecture. Although the site's chronology is not precisely defined, its prominent remains are associated with the Late Classic. Hochob's relatively compact hilltop setting allows the relationship between decoration, enclosed rooms and the surrounding plaza to be understood at an intimate scale.

The hilltop was deliberately levelled to make room for connected plazas, houses and ceremonial buildings. INAH’s guide places Hochob’s strongest architectural flowering around AD 850–1000. Its small size does not diminish the complexity of its stone façades. Structure II’s entrance turns the entire doorway into an enormous sacred mouth, with teeth, ear ornaments and stacked profile masks integrated into the masonry.

Early descriptions record a decorated roof-comb above this building, most of which has disappeared. Another group combines Chenes-style imagery with towers and simulated stairways associated with Río Bec architecture. Openings beside the buildings lead to underground rainwater cisterns. These reservoirs help explain how a community sustained itself on a raised limestone site without a permanent surface water supply.

sources.author: Renée Lorelei Zapata Peraza

site-5008.description:
Oxkintok lies near the northwestern edge of the Puuc hills, where its buildings preserve a long sequence of architectural change. It was among the early important centres of the northern lowlands and has dated inscriptions from the Classic period. The enclosed passages of the Satunsat, often described as a labyrinth, give the site an unusual architectural focus. Other groups show the development of regional Puuc forms. Its hill-country setting and different building phases make Oxkintok particularly valuable for tracing how the monumental traditions of northern Yucatán developed over time.

Oxkintok's architecture records a long sequence of experimentation. The INAH guide follows changes from early regional forms toward the better-known Puuc tradition, including improvements in stone cutting and vault construction. Its principal Ah Dzib, Ah May and Ah Canul groups concentrate buildings on large platforms connected by causeways, while smaller groups extend around them.

The Satunsat is especially distinctive: a multilevel building with a maze-like arrangement of vaulted passages and chambers, partly adapted to the underlying rock. Small wall openings admitted light or air; proposed astronomical and cosmological functions remain interpretations. Later offerings and alterations in the Ah Canul Group show that some places continued to matter after the city's political importance diminished. Oxkintok thus preserves both changing architectural techniques and the reuse of established sacred settings.

sources.label: INAH · Oxkintok archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Luis Raúl Pantoja Díaz , Diseñador (dsr): Manuel Cózar

site-5010.description: Chacmultun spreads across hills and terraces in the Puuc region of Yucatán. Its principal groups include Chacmultun, Cabalpak and Xetpol, with buildings positioned to accentuate their height above the surrounding terrain. Decorated masonry friezes identify the Puuc architectural tradition, while traces of painted interiors add another dimension to the surviving stonework. The reddish appearance of its buildings gives the site its modern name. Occupation began before its Late Classic architectural flowering and continued into later centuries.

site-5028.description: Plan de Ayutla occupies a hilly setting in the upper Usumacinta region. Its architectural complexes include evidence interpreted as a space for elite theatrical performance, adding to the better-known palatial and ceremonial remains. The site's ancient identity has been debated, with different proposed links to names found in inscriptions elsewhere. Those identifications remain distinct from the securely located archaeological remains. Its monumental plan is therefore presented without assigning an uncertain ancient kingdom name as fact.

site-5030.description: Nakum stands near the Holmul River within the Yaxhá–Nakum–Naranjo region. Its monumental architecture includes a well-preserved temple roof comb and extensive palatial groups. The city flourished in the later Classic centuries, when river routes supported communication and exchange. Archaeological work examines how its growth related to the changing fortunes of larger neighbouring kingdoms. The source survey point is approximate; the archaeological narrative describes the wider settlement rather than a precise visitor entrance.

site-5032.description: Yaxhá occupies a ridge between lakes Yaxhá and Sacnab in eastern Petén. Its name, associated with blue-green water, is a rare example of an ancient Maya place-name surviving into modern use. The city developed through a long occupation, with major expansion in the Early Classic and later competition with nearby Naranjo. Hundreds of structures include ceremonial groups joined by raised causeways, as well as carved stelae. The lake setting helps explain both its prominence and its connections: this was a substantial political centre within a landscape of waterways, routes and neighbouring kingdoms.

site-5036.description: Lubaantún's broad platforms and rounded corners distinguish it from many better-known Maya centres. Large fitted blocks were laid without mortar, and the surviving upper platforms lack the stone temple rooms common elsewhere, suggesting that some superstructures used perishable materials. The city flourished during a relatively short span of the Late Classic in southern Belize. Finds include numerous miniature ceramic objects and evidence of ballcourts. Its raised setting between streams and unusual masonry make Lubaantún a useful reminder of the variety within Maya architecture, rather than a variation on a single standard pyramid form.

site-5079.description: El Palmar was a substantial city in southeastern Campeche with a long history of monumental construction and regional diplomacy. The Guzmán Group is particularly important for evidence concerning officials known as lakam, whose roles included representing the court in wider political networks. Hieroglyphic records help connect a residential group with events beyond the city. This account belongs to the Campeche settlement; several other survey records share the name El Palmar.

site-5127.description: Uxul was a substantial city southwest of Calakmul, with occupation beginning in the Preclassic and major growth during the Classic period. Inscriptions connect its ruling elite to Calakmul’s Kaanul dynasty, including a panel depicting a Calakmul king in a ballgame setting. Palace burials and ceramic offerings provide evidence for differences in elite status. Large engineered reservoirs reveal another side of urban life: the labour and planning required to store water through the seasonal dry months of the interior lowlands.

site-5153.description:
Toniná's monumental centre climbs a hillside in successive terraces, joining palaces, temples and courtyards into a great acropolis. Its rulers competed with other Maya powers, and sculptures of captives record the place of warfare in royal display. The complex includes the Palace of the Fireflies, with rooms around courtyards and evidence of water management, as well as elaborate stucco reliefs. Temples occupy the highest levels. Rather than a single isolated pyramid, Toniná presents an interconnected architectural slope, where ascent through different spaces was central to the experience of the city.

Toniná's Acropolis is a densely organized architectural landscape. Seven rising platforms carry courts, passages, palaces and temples, with successive stairways controlling access as people moved upward. In his INAH guide, archaeologist Juan Yadeun Angulo interprets this arrangement as a ceremonial ordering of space tied to celestial cycles; that symbolic reading is an interpretation of the architecture rather than a surviving written plan.

The palace areas preserve suites of rooms around interior courts, alongside more austere ranges elsewhere in the complex. Sculpture and modeled stucco made political and ritual messages part of these surroundings, including representations of captives and cosmic imagery. The ballcourt occupied a lower space beside the watercourse. Later reuse altered buildings and monuments after the city's principal royal period, so damaged sculptures and architectural modifications also belong to Toniná's long history.

site-5187.description:
Ichkabal is an extensive ancient settlement in the forest west of Bacalar, near Dzibanché. Large platforms and pyramidal complexes document substantial monumental construction beginning before the Classic period. Its proximity and architectural connections place it within the wider history of southern Quintana Roo and the Kaan dynasty's region. The scale of the principal groups is especially notable, while much of the broader urban landscape requires archaeological investigation beyond its most visible monuments.

The 2025 INAH guide presents Ichkabal as a landscape of monumental platforms, plazas, causeways and engineered water storage. Structures 4 and 5 are triadic acropolises, each arranging three temples on a raised platform. At Structure 5, superimposed stairways reveal successive construction stages, while surviving stucco masks retain evidence of the buildings’ former decoration. Much of the immense Structure 1 remains beneath vegetation.

Beside the main plaza, an artificial reservoir known as the Crocodile Pool provided stored water and now supports wetland wildlife. Offerings associated with Structure 7 included Pacific shells and jade from Guatemala, connecting this inland settlement with wider exchange networks. The guide also describes an E-Group arrangement used to mark solar events. Such evidence links architecture with ritual, seasonal observation and the practical demands of urban life.
